description_en: The Vajrayoginī Temple in Sankhu is one of the four yoginī deities of the Kathmandu Valley and is revered as the guardian deity of the town. Located west of the Jogeśvara Mandira (SKH0510), the three-tiered temple faces south and has a roof covered in gilt-copper sheets with a finial on top. Interestingly, both Vajrayoginī and Jogeśvara Temples are believed to be standing on a single rock, without a proper foundation.The entrance to the sanctum of the Temple has a decorative covering of gilded sheets along with thetoraṇaabove it. Rājarājeśvarīdevī, the queen of Raṇa Bahādura Śāha, offered the door,toraṇa, and window to Vajrayoginī in 1799 CE (VS 1856) (D. Vajrācārya and Ṭ. Śreṣṭha2037, p. 306-307;D. Sharma and T. Shrestha2016, p. 431-432). Theṭoraṇahas an eight-armed goddess in a dancing posture at the center. Although the form of the deity on theṭoraṇais different from Vajrayoginī at the sanctum, she is also revered as Vajrayoginī.[1]The statue of Vajrayoginī has three eyes and a red face. Therefore, she is also revered as Hyāũkhvāḥmāju (lit. red-faced deity). Traditionally, Vajrayoginī carried avajrain her right palm, but after defeating Śaṅkarācārya, an 8th-century ascetic and philosopher, in a doctrinal debate, she buried hervajrain her womb and began carrying a sword (khaḍga) instead. Since then, she has been known as Khaḍgayoginī. The rest of her body is covered with a cloth.[2]Siṃhinī and Heruka are enshrined to the west of Vajrayoginī, while Vyāghrinī and Acalā can be found to the east. In front of the temple to the southwest is a large stone encircled by Vāsukī Nāga, a serpent deity, which is worshipped by priests as Akṣobhya. There is also a small terracotta temple located to the west of the Vajrayoginī Temple, where an upright statue of Buddha used to be enshrined. Some believe the statue to belong to the 13th century and worship it as Nemuni, while others revere it as Mañjuśrī. Thus, the temple is sometimes referred to as the Mañjuśrī Temple. After the statue was stolen in 1985 CE, a smaller replica was installed, and a statue of Sarasvatī was also placed next to it.She carries a khaḍga with her right hand and a blue lotus with the left. Usually, deities are seen holding a khaḍga with their palm. However, Vajrayoginī does not hold the khaḍga, but the emblem is tied to her fingers with a piece of cloth. She originally carried a vajra with her right palm. After she defeated Śaṅkarācārya, a renowned ascetic and philosopher of the 8th century, in a doctrinal debate, she buried her vajra in her womb and held a khaḍga. Since then, she also came to be known as Khaḍgayoginī. The rest of her body is covered with a cloth.[2]Siṃhinī and Heruka are enshrined to the west of Vajrayoginī, while Vyāghrinī and Acalā can be found to the east. In front of the temple to the southwest is a large stone encircled by Vāsukī Nāga, a serpent deity, which is worshipped by priests as Akṣobhya. There is also a small terracotta temple located to the west of the Vajrayoginī Temple, where an upright statue of Buddha used to be enshrined. Some believe the statue to belong to the 13th century (L. Bangdel1989, p. 147) and worship it as Nemuni, while others revere it as Mañjuśrī. Thus, the temple is sometimes referred to as the Mañjuśrī Temple. After the statue was stolen in 1985 CE ((B. Shrestha2012, p. 419),), a smaller replica was installed, and a statue of Sarasvatī was also placed next to it.The origin story of the Goddess Vajrayoginī is detailed in the Maṇiśaila Mahāvadāna, a Buddhist scripture, theMaṇiśailaMahāvadāna. It tells of how, during the Satya Yuga, the first of the four ages of the world in the present cosmic age known as the Bhadrakalpa, Vajrayoginī manifested from a divine ray of five colors emanating from a space between two stones named Maṇiśilā (lit. large stone of jewel), which were located on the Maṇicūḍa (lit. jewel like a tuft of hair [on top of the head]) Hillock. As her divine ray brightened every corner, all the creatures revered her for ages. Jñānācārya, a person who abstained from worldly pleasures, understood her powers and began to worship her regularly. The deity appeared before him in her divine form and appointed him as her priest. Jñānācārya came to be known as Vācāsiddhi Vajrācārya, and his son Jyotideva Vajrācārya succeeded him as the priest, performing daily rituals at the shrine of Vajrayoginī. Later, Jogadeva Vajrācārya, the 9th-generation descendant of Vācāsiddhi Vajrācārya, founded the town of Sankhu. The Licchavi King Vṛṣadeva was also a pious devotee of Vajrayoginī and offered her food before eating himself (as mentioned in the (Nepālikabhūpavaṃśāvali12.38).No historic source is available that shed light on the initial construction of the temple. However, it is known that the tiered Temple of Vajrayoginī was previously aśikhara-style structure. It is unclear if the Temple was constructed in a different style before that. In 1655 CE (NS 775), King Pratāpa Malla commissioned the construction of a temple for Vajrayoginī and endowed lands for aguthito observe the daily rituals at the temple (D. Sharma and T. Shrestha2016, p. 408-412). The inscription that records this event does not clearly specify the style in which the temple was constructed. However, it does mention a practice of coating the temple with lime every year on the full moon day of Caitra. A tiered temple does not require lime coats. This suggests that the temple Pratāpa Malla got constructed was in theśikharastyle. A later-reconstruction of the temple in 1670 CE (NS 790) saw the installation of a finial (T. Siṃha1136, 4, folio 4B). It is not possible that a finial was installed 15 years after the construction of the Temple in 1655 CE.The Temple was probably rebuilt before the installation of a finial. Unfortunately, there are no historic sources that clarify this confusion. An entry in an annal mentions that thecakrainstalled on the northern side of theśikhara-style (granthakūṭa) Temple of Vajrayoginī fell off in 1683 CE (NS 803) (T. Siṃha1136, p. 12, folio 17B). This makes it clear that it was aśikhara-style Temple till at least 1683 CE. Later in 1712 CE (NS 832), Kathmandu's King Bhāṣkara Malla and his mother got theśikhara-style Temple dismantled and rebuilt it as a tiered structure (G. Vajrācārya2023, p. 33). The Temple was renovated by Friends of Sankhu, a local organization, with the funds from the Netherlands arranged by the efforts of Bālagopāla Śreṣṭha and the late Bert van den Hoek in 2002 CE. The Temple did not collapse in the 2015 earthquakes but was left with multiple cracks. Wooden supports were placed all around the Temple to prevent it from collapsing. The Department of Archaeology rebuilt both Vajrayoginī and Jogeśvara Temples at a total cost of NRs. 59.2 million.The priest of Jogeśvara Temple is responsible for performing daily rituals at the Vajrayoginī Temple. While four daily rituals are observed at the Jogeśvara Temple, only two are performed at the Vajrayoginī Temple. Daily worship takes place early in the morning, and an āratī is offered in the evening. Every year, the Vajrayoginī Jātrā is celebrated for eight days in Sankhu, beginning on the full moon day of Caitra. The Mhāsukhvāḥmāju Dyaḥchẽ (SKH0550) houses replicas of Vajrayoginī, Siṃhinī (the lion-faced deity), and Vyāghrinī (the tiger-faced deity). On the fourth day of the dark fortnight of Vaiśākha, a procession featuring the statues of Mhāsukhvāḥmāju, Siṃhinī, Vyāghrinī, Svayambhū Caitya, and Vasundharā takes place. On the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Vaiśākha, the statues are brought back to the Dyaḥchẽ, marking the end of the Jātrā. Once every 12 years, the face of Vajrayoginī is repaired and repainted in a ritual known as lãpu chāygu. In case of any damages, such repair works are carried out even before the 12 years. It used to be carried out every year, but King Śivadeva arranged for the ritual painting to be performed every 12 years (Nepālikabhūpavaṃśāvali12.148). Vajrayoginī is revered as the lineage deity by caste groups such as Rāṇās, Thāpās, Basnyāts, etc., who frequently visit the temple to worship their lineage deity.[1]According toB. Bhattacharyya1958, p. 248-249, the deity enshrined at the sanctum is not Vajrayoginī. She is Ugratārādevī, who is also known as Mahācīnatārā. When East Bengal was defeated following the invasion of the Muslim army of Mohammedan, the Bengali priests from Ḍakkā (currently known as Dhaka, the capital of Bangladesh) came to Nepal with the statue of Ugratārā. This suggests that the statue of Ugratārā brought by the Bengalis is being worshipped as Vajrayoginī in Sankhu. Bhattacharyya does not give the source of this account.[2]The priests are reluctant to disclose the material the statue of Vajrayoginī is made of. They fear that disclosing it will strike them with the evil eyes of the deity.
description_ne: साँखुको जोगेश्वर मन्दिर (SKH0510)को पश्चिममा वज्रयोगिनी मन्दिर रहेको छ । काठमाडौं उपत्यकाका चार योगिनीहरूमध्ये साँखुको वज्रयोगिनी पनि एक हो । वज्रयोगिनीलाई साँखुको रक्षक देवीको रूपमा सम्मानपूर्वक पूजा गरिन्छ । वज्रयोगिनी र जोगेश्वर दुबै मन्दिरको जग छैन । दुबै मन्दिर एउटै सिंगो ढुङ्गामाथि बनाइएको मानिन्छ । दक्षिणाभिमुखी गरी बनाइएको यो मन्दिर तीन तलाको छ । मन्दिरको गर्भगृहभित्र प्रवेश गर्ने ढोका र उक्त ढोकामाथिको तोरणमा सुनको मोलम्बा लगाइएको छ । रणबहादुर शाहकी रानी राजराजेश्वरीदेवीले विसं १८५६ (सन् १७९९) मा ढोका, तोरण र झ्याल चढाएकी थिइन् (D. Vajrācārya and Ṭ. Śreṣṭha2037, p. 306-307;D. Sharma and T. Shrestha2016, p. 431-432) । तोरणको मध्य भागमा आठ हात भएकी नृत्य मुद्रामा रहेको देवी राखिएको छ । गर्भगृहभित्र रहेको मूर्तिभन्दा तोरणमा राखिएको मूर्ति फरक भएपनि यिनलाई पनि वज्रयोगिनी नै मानिन्छ । मन्दिरको गर्भगृहभित्र वज्रयोगिनीको मूर्ति स्थापना गरिएको छ ।[1]वज्रयोगिनीको अनुहार रातो छ र तीनवटा आँखा बनाइएका छन् । उनको दायाँ हातमा खड्ग र बायाँ हातमा नीलोत्पल रहेको छ । सामान्यतया देवीदेवताहरूले खड्ग समातेका हुन्छन्, तर यहाँ वज्रयोगिनीले खड्ग समातेका छैनन्, कपडाले देवीको औंलामा खड्ग बाँधिएको छ । पहिले उनले दायाँ हातमा वज्र धारण गरेका थिए, पछि शङ्कराचार्यलाई शास्त्रार्थमा पराजित गरेपछि आफ्नो वज्रलाई गर्भमा राखी खड्ग धारण गरेका थिए । त्यस बेलादेखि उनलाई खड्गयोगिनी पनि भन्न थालिएको हो । शरीरमा कपडाले छोपेकोले अन्य भागहरू देखिँदैनन् ।[2]वज्रयोगिनीको पश्चिममा सिंहिनी र हेरुक राखिएका छन् भने पूर्वमा व्याघ्रिनी र अचला राखिएका छन् । मन्दिर अगाडि दक्षिण-पश्चिमतिर वासुकी नागले घेरिएको ठूलो ढुङ्गा रहेको छ । मन्दिरका पूजारीहरू त्यस ढुङ्गालाई अक्षोभ्य बुद्ध मानी पूजा गर्छन् । मन्दिरको पश्चिममा टेराकोटाले बनेको सानो मन्दिर छ । त्यस मन्दिरभित्र उभिएको बुद्धको मूर्ति थियो ।L. Bangdel(1989, p. 147) ले त्यस मूर्तलाई १३औं शताब्दीको मानेका छन् । त्यस मूर्तिलाई कसैले नेमुनि मान्छन् भने कसैले मञ्जुश्री मान्छन् । त्यस मूर्तिलाई मञ्जुश्री मान्दै टेराकोटाको त्यस सानो मन्दिरलाई मञ्जुश्री मन्दिर भनी सम्बोधन गरिएको पाइन्छ । सन् १९८५ मा उक्त मूर्ति चोरी भएपछि (B. Shrestha2012, p. 419) भित्तामा त्यसकै प्रतिकृति स्वरूप सानो मूर्ति राखिएको छ । मन्दिरको भित्तामा सरस्वतीको पनि मूर्ति राखिएको छ ।वज्रयोगिनीको स्थापनाबारे मणिशैल महावदानमा वर्णन गरिएको छ । भद्रकल्पको सत्ययुगमा मणिचूड पर्वतमा रहेका मणिशिला नामक दुई ढुङ्गाको कापबाट निस्किएको पञ्चरश्मि ज्वालाबाट वज्रयोगिनीको उत्पत्ति भएको मानिन्छ । उक्त ज्वालाको कारणले सर्वत्र उज्यालो भएकोले सम्पूर्ण चराचर प्राणीले कैयौं कालमसम्म उग्रतारा वज्रयोगिनीको आराधना गरिरहे । वज्रयोगिनीको महिमा बुझेर योगी ज्ञानाचार्यले दिनहुँ उनको पूजा गर्न थाले । देवीले योगी ज्ञानाचार्यलाई दर्शन दिई आफ्नो पूजारीको रूपमा नियुक्त गरेकी थिइन् । उनै योगी ज्ञानाचार्य पूजारीको नाम पछि वाचासिद्धि वज्राचार्य रहन गएको हो । त्यसपछि वाचासिद्धि वज्राचार्यका छोरा ज्योतिदेव वज्राचार्य वज्रयोगिनीदेवीको नित्यपूजा गर्ने पूजारी भए । वाचासिद्धि वज्राचार्यका सन्तान दरसन्तानमध्ये नवौं पुस्ताका जोगदेव वज्राचार्यले साँखु शहर स्थापना गरेका थिए । लिच्छवि राजा वृषदेव वज्रयोगिनीका भक्त थिए र देवीलाई भोजन गराइसकेपछि मात्र आफू भोजन गर्थे(Nepālikabhūpavaṃśāvali12.38) ।मन्दिरको प्रारम्भिक इतिहासबारे जानकारी दिने ऐतिहासिक स्रोत उपलब्ध छैन । अहिले यो मन्दिर तल्ले शैलीको भएपनि पहिले शिखरकूट शैलीको थियो भन्ने कुरा चाहिँ थाहा पाइन्छ । शिखरकूट शैलीको मन्दिरभन्दा अघि कुन शैलीको मन्दिर थियो भन्ने कुरा थाहा पाइँदैन । नेसं ७७५ (सन् १६५५) राजा प्रताप मल्लले वज्रयोगिनीको लागि मन्दिर निर्माण गरी नित्यपूजाको लागि जग्गा गुठी राखिदिएका थिए (D. Sharma and T. Shrestha2016, p. 408-412) । उक्त मन्दिर कुन शैलीमा निर्माण गरिएको थियो भन्ने कुरा अभिलेखबाट खुल्दैन । प्रत्येक वर्ष चैत्र शुक्ल पूर्णिमाको दिनमा मन्दिरमा चुना लगाउनुपर्ने व्यवस्था गरिएको छ । तल्ले शैलीको मन्दिरमा चुना लगाउनुपर्ने आवश्यकता हुँदैन । त्यसैले प्रताप मल्लले बनाएको त्यो मन्दिर शिखरकूट शैलीको हुनसक्ने सम्भावना देखिन्छ । नेसं ७९० (सन् १६७०) मा पछि निर्माण गरिएको वज्रयोगिनीको मन्दिरमा गजूर चढाइएको थियो (T. Siṃha1136, 4, folio 4B) । प्रताप मल्लले नेसं ७७५ (सन् १६५५) मा मन्दिर बनाइसकेपछि १५ वर्षपछि मात्र गजूर चढाएको हुनसक्दैन । त्यस बीचमा मन्दिरको पुनर्निर्माण गरिएको वा पुनः नयाँ मन्दिर बनाएर गजूर चढाएको हुनसक्छ । यो अन्यौललाई प्रष्ट पार्ने ऐतिहासिक सामग्री भेटिएको छैन । घटनावलीमा टिपिए अनुसार नेसं ८०३ (सन् १६८३) मा वज्रयोगिनीको ग्रन्थकूट (शिखरकूट) मन्दिरको उत्तरपट्टि राखिएको चक्र खसेको थियो (T. Siṃha1136, p. 12, folio 17B)। यसबाट नेसं नेसं ८०३ (सन् १६८३) सम्म वज्रयोगिनीको मन्दिर शिखरकूट शैलीमा बनाइएको प्रष्ट हुन्छ । काठमाडौंका राजा भाष्कर मल्ल र उनकी आमाले पहिलेको ग्रन्थकूट (शिखरकूट) मन्दिरलाई भत्काएर  नेसं ८३२ (सन् १७१२) कार्तिक कृष्ण प्रतिपदामा तल्ले शैलीको मन्दिरको निर्माण कार्य सम्पन्न गरी गजूर चढाएका थिए (G. Vajrācārya2023, p. 33) । नेसं ११२२ (सन् २००२) मा बालगोपाल श्रेष्ठ र दिवंगत Bert van den Hoek को संयुक्त प्रयासबाट Netherlands बाट आर्थिक सहयोग जुटाई Friends of Sankhu नामक संस्थाले मन्दिरको जीर्णोद्धार गरेको थियो । विसं २०७२ (सन् २०१५) को भूकम्पले मन्दिरमा क्षति पुगेको थियो । मन्दिर नभत्केपनि धेरै ठाउँमा चर्केको थियो र मन्दिर नभत्कियोस् भनेर टेको राख्नुपरेको थियो । भूकम्पले क्षति पुगेको वज्रयोगिनी मन्दिर र जोगेश्वर मन्दिरको पुरातत्व विभागबाट एकैपल्ट पुनर्निर्माण गरिएको थियो । पुनर्निर्माण गर्दा दुबै मन्दिरको गरी जम्मा ५ करोड ९२ लाख खर्च भएको थियो । संस्कृति, पर्यटन तथा नागरिक उड्डयन मन्त्री योगेश भट्टराईले मन्दिरको उद्घाटन गरेका थिए ।प्रत्येक दिन जोगेश्वर मन्दिरमा नित्यपूजा गर्ने पूजारीले यस मन्दिरमा पनि पूजा गर्छन् । जोगेश्वर मन्दिरमा दिनको चारपल्ट पूजा गरेपनि वज्रयोगिनी मन्दिरमा दिनको दुईपल्ट मात्र पूजा गरिन्छ । बिहान सबेरै नित्यपूजा गरिन्छ भने बेलुकी आरती दिइन्छ । प्रत्येक वर्ष चैत्र शुक्ल पूर्णिमादेखि आठ दिनसम्म वज्रयोगिनीको खटजात्रा मनाइन्छ । मन्दिरको गर्भगृहमा राखिएका वज्रयोगिनी, सिंघिनी र व्याघ्रिनीको मूर्तिको प्रतिरूप बनाएर म्हासुख्वाःमाजु द्यःछेँ (SKH0550) मा राखिएका छन् । जात्राको चौथो दिन वैशाख कृष्ण ३ मा द्यःछेँमा राखिएका म्हासुख्वाःमाजु (वज्रयोगिनी), सिंहिनी, व्याघ्रिनी, स्वयम्भू चैत्य र वसुन्धरालाई खटमा राखेर जात्रा गरिन्छ । वैशाख कृष्ण ८ मा देवतालाई पुनः द्यःछेँमा ल्याएर विधिपूर्वक स्थापना गरिन्छ । प्रत्येक १२ वर्षमा वज्रयोगिनीको मुहार मर्मत गरी रंगरोगन गरिन्छ । त्यस कार्यलाई नेवारीमालँपु छायेगुभनिन्छ । मूर्तिमा कुनै टुटफुट भएमा १२ वर्ष हुनुभन्दा अगाडि नै रंगरोगन गरिन्छ । पहिले वर्षैपिच्छे लँपु छायेगु गरिन्थ्यो, पछि राजा शिवदेवको पालामा १२ वर्षमा एकपल्ट गर्नैपर्ने परम्परा बसालिएको थियो (Nepālikabhūpavaṃśāvali12.148) । राणा, थापा, बस्न्यात् आदि समुदायले वज्रयोगिनीलाई आफ्नो कुलदेवीका रूपमा पूज्दै आएका छन् । ती खलकका मानिसहरू कुलदेवता पूजा गर्न आइरहन्छन् ।[1]B. Bhattacharyya(1958, p. 248-249) का अनुसार वज्रयोगिनी भनिएपनि गर्भगृहभित्र स्थापना गरिएको मूर्ति वज्रयोगिनीको होइन्, उग्रतारादेवीको हो जसलाई महाचीनताराको नामले पनि चिनिन्छ । सन् १३५० तिर मुहम्मदनको सेनाले भारतको पूर्वी बंगालमा आक्रमण गरी विजय हासिल गरेपछि डक्का (हालको बंगलादेशको राजधानी ढाका) मा बस्ने बंगाली पूजारीहरूले उग्रताराको मूर्तिलाई आफूसित लिएर नेपाल प्रवेश गरेका थिए । यस विवरणबाट बंगालीहरूले ल्याएको उग्रताराको मूर्तिलाई नै साँखुमा वज्रयोगिनी मानी पूजा गरिरहेको देखिन्छ । भट्टाचार्यले यसको कुनै स्रोत खुलाएका छैनन् ।[2]वज्रयोगिनीको मूर्ति के ले बनेको हो भन्ने कुरा खोल्न पूजारीहरू तैयार छैनन् । त्यो कुरा अरुलाई भनेमा देवीको कुदृष्टि पर्छ भन्ने डर उनीहरूमा रहेको छ ।

historical_events.event_description: The Bhoṭes, who are of Tibetan origin, forcibly opened the door of the Vajrayoginī Temple and stole the jewelry belonging to the deity. Upon discovering the theft, Priest Bābudeva reported the incident to King Amṛta Malla, who took action and successfully apprehended the thieves. As a part of purification process, a ritual was performed since the thieves had touched the statue of the deity.

King Pratāpa Malla initiated the construction of the temple and allocated lands for aguthito oversee the daily rituals at the site. Although the inscription documenting this event does not explicitly specify the architectural style of the temple, it does reference an annual tradition of applying lime to the temple on the full moon day of Caitra. Given that lime coatings are unnecessary for tiered temples, this suggests that the temple erected by Pratāpa Malla followed theśikharastyle. The inscription is divided into two separate steles, with the first one  positioned north of the Jogeśvara Mandira, and the second one affixed to the west-facing wall of the Jogeśvara Mandira.

historical_events.event_name: Offering pinnacle to the later temple
historical_events.event_description: A later reconstruction of the Temple, dated to 1670 CE (NS 790), included the installation of a finial. However, it is unlikely that a finial was added just 15 years after the initial construction of the Temple in 1655 CE. It is possible that the Temple was rebuilt prior to the addition of the finial, but there are no historical sources available to confirm this hypothesis.

The process of repairing and repainting the face of Vajrayoginī began on the 11th day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna, with the removal of her vital essence from the statue. This event, known as (Nev.)lãpu chāygu,lasted for a month until life was ritually placed back into the statue on the 11th day of the bright fortnight of Caitra.

Jayadharma and Ugramāla Malla presented King Pratāpa Malla with 398tolāsof sterling silver and 229tolāsof pure silver as a contribution towards making atoraṇa. It is likely that the silver was deposited at the temple by various devotees on separate occasions as offerings to the deity.
King Pratāpa Malla offered a goldentoraṇato Vajrayoginī. A silvertoraṇamade out of the silver deposited at the Temple was also offered to the deity on the same occasion.
A special ritual for auspiciousness was performed after the blue lotus on the left hand of Vajrayoginī was broken.
During the reign of King Nṛpendra Malla, the vital essence of of Vajrayoginī was removed from her statue to repair and repaint her face.

The Vajrayoginī Temple experienced strange noises resembling the sound of large utensils falling, but the source of the noises could not be determined. King Pārthivendra Malla was notified of the incident, and a special ritual for auspiciousness was performed in response.
The vital essence of Vajrayoginīwas removed from the statue to repair and repaint her face.

The Gũ Bāhāḥ premises were struck by lightning. Fortunately, the priest of the temple was unharmed as he lay prostrate on the ground. However, when the Temple's door was opened the following day, soot marks were observed on the statue of temple andits left earring (kuṇḍala).
Thecakrainstalled on the northern side of theśikhara-style (granthakūṭa) Temple of Vajrayoginī fell off.
Naka Mayaju, Queen of King Pārthivendra Malla, offered atoraṇato Vajrayoginī along with utensils required for the worship of the deity.
The vital essence was removed from the statue of Vajrayoginī to repair and repaint her face.
The inscription at the Vajrayoginī Temple is eroded, making it unclear what event took place there.Something was done at the Vajrayoginī Temple.

historical_events.event_name: Converting Śikharakūṭa temple into tiered temple
historical_events.event_description: Kathmandu's King Bhāṣkara Malla and his mother got theśikhara-style Temple dismantled and rebuilt it in a tiered structure. They also offered a finial on that occasion.

A band of invaders from Bhaktapur, under the leadership of Nīlanārāyaṇa Thakura, infiltrated Sankhu. However, bolstered by the blessings of Vajrayoginī, King Jagajjaya Malla mobilized the citizens of Sankhu, ultimately repelling the invaders and killing 16 of them. The remaining 17 aggressors were subsequently apprehended and escorted as captives to Kathmandu.

historical_events.event_name: Endowment of land to the Vajrayoginī Mandira
historical_events.event_description: King Jagajjaya Malla expressed his gratitude to Vajrayoginī for her blessings during the victory over the invaders from Bhaktapur by endowing land for aguthidedicated to the goddess.
A certain individual, named Mati, resident of Obhu, offered a 72-cubit longbanner (patāḥ)to Vajrayoginī.
Scores of termites were observed inside the Vajrayoginī Temple for two consecutive days. Following consultation with holy scriptures, special worship rituals for auspiciousness were conducted.

historical_events.event_name: Offering of a door, window and toraṇa.
historical_events.event_description: During the reign of Raṇa Bahādura Śāha, his queen Rājarājeśvarīdevī made an offering to the Vajrayoginī Temple.She generously donated a decorative covering crafted from gilded sheets for the entrance to the sanctum, along with atoraṇapositioned above it, and a window.

historical_events.event_name: Offering of a stone pillar with a lion statue
historical_events.event_description: Tejanārāyaṇa Tulādhara, a resident of Madu (also known as Maru) Ṭola of Kathmandu, along with his wife Viṣṇumati and other family members, made a generous offering to the Vajrayoginī Temple. They donated a stone pillar adorned with a gilt copper lion figure, which was erected in front of the temple.
Commander Colonel Keśarasiṃha offered a metal frill to the Vajrayoginī Temple together with his wife and family members.
The inscription documents the establishment of adharmadhātu maṇḍalaat the Vajrayoginī temple, however, it omits the name of the donor.

A theft took place at the Vajrayoginī Temple when a group of individuals arrived in a vehicle, armed with pistols. Local residents attempted to apprehend the thieves, resulting in two individuals being shot and injured by the assailants. Eventually, the thieves were apprehended along with the stolen items and turned over to the police.
Erosion has deteriorated the stone stele to the extent that the inscription is now illegible.
The inscription has suffered significant damage and is illegible.

historical_events.event_name: Donation to the Vajrayoginī  Service Committee
historical_events.event_description: Several individuals provided financial contributions to the Vajrayoginī Sevā Sudhāra Samiti (Vajrayoginī Service Committee), a local organization dedicated to the preservation of the temple.
The Friends of Sankhu, a local organization, restored the temple using funds from the Netherlands, which were arranged through the efforts of Bālagopāla Śreṣṭha and the late Bert van den Hoek.

During the 2015 earthquakes, the Vajrayoginī Temple sustained multiple cracks but fortunately did not collapse. To prevent further damage or collapse, wooden supports were placed all around the temple.
The Department of Archaeology rebuilt both Vajrayoginī and Jogeśvaratemples at a total cost of NRs. 59.2 million.
